# Building AI Companions from Scratch: A Practical Guide to Creating Your Own AI Companion with Rust and Burn

# Our Agenda

This book will walk us through the creation of a virtual pet (AI companion) called Yumon. That is how we will learn the practical knowledge necessary to train transformer models. I have provided a base dataset to help you get started immediately, and it is easy to change to fit your own personality. We will be writing our code in Rust, but you do not need to know Rust to follow along. All of the code is already written and available on GitHub, so you can download (clone) it and edit without requiring complex knowledge. However, if you are a programmer, you can evolve the code in a deeper way. Have fun\!

# Why Rust and Burn

Let’s briefly discuss the primary motivations for our chosen tech stack. Choosing your tech stack will matter immensely when it comes to a number of factors including reliability, capability, portability, and performance.  
We choose Rust for a number of reasons. The first reason is that Burn requires Rust, and we have very good reasons for using Burn. However, Rust is also highly ergonomic in its syntax, even if a bit tricky to learn in terms of its data ownership paradigm. Rust is fast and secure. Perhaps most importantly, Rust is highly portable just like Burn. That means you can write any kind of application in Rust, so you can share code and be more efficient. Rust can run on basically any device, including edge devices like a toaster. Although, it would have to be a toaster you are quite familiar with\!  
Even more crucial to our goals is the choice of the Burn machine learning framework. This framework is insanely fast while offering extreme portability. That means you can deploy a Burn model basically anywhere, be it the cloud, your local computer, an edge device, or even the browser. It’s important to note that some competing frameworks in the Python community exist, such as PyTorch. PyTorch, due to its more highly-optimized kernels, is actually faster at training than Burn. PyTorch also comes with more modules out of the box, such as its own flash attention implementation. However, PyTorch suffers from high reliance on CUDA GPUs made by Nvidia, making it very low-portability. This means we can’t deploy our model wherever we wish\! PyTorch is also a large download.

# Cloning the Code

Now has come time to ensure that you have access to the latest code which we will be using and walking through in this book. This is essential to getting the most out of this book, as all of the practical lessons will be pointless without a reference to look at. You can find the code repository at this URL: [https://github.com/alexthegoodman/yumon-pet](https://github.com/alexthegoodman/yumon-pet) and it is completely free to obtain the code. The README file contains some helpful information to get you started.

# Easy Data Creation

Included in the archive folder of the GitHub repository, you will find a handful of handcrafted datasets. These are the best kind by far. Downloading or scraping datasets is not going to get you the same end quality in terms of model outputs. Although distilling from an open source model is a quality secondary source. With only a couple thousand handcrafted chat samples, you can achieve decent, if somewhat garbled outputs. If you supplement with distilled data of a larger volume, you will get even more fluent and coherent responses due to the data volume. It will also take fewer epochs of training time.  
I recommend that you open these files and edit their contents to fit your own personality. I am interested in God, video games, music, and hard work, so that is what most of the chats are about. You may wish to keep most of the odd statements and questions, and simply replace the trained Yumon responses.  
These trained responses can be memorized at times by the model, which produces a “perfect” output, but does not convey the model’s personal opinions, thoughts, or feelings as would happen when they generalize. When they generalize, the connections which they formed come to the surface, just as with a human, in the form of opinions and statements. While generalized outputs can be choppy at our smaller scale, they are still relevant and intelligible to the right audience.  
The chats look something like this:

`What is the universe?`  
`The universe is a wide open space filled with planets.`  
`What is a planet?`  
`A planet is a large ball floating in space.`  
`What is a wide open space?`  
`Open space is an empty area where nothing exists.`

`Tell me more about the universe`  
`Sure, the universe has many stars and planets`  
`How many stars and planets are there?`  
`There are billions of them in space`  
`Can we reach any of these planets?`  
`We can only reach the planets in our solar system`

# Downloading Data

There are going to be times where you want to try another dataset to see what kinds of results you can get. There is a good reason to do this. If you have enough data and a high enough capacity on your model, then you can certainly consider it because your model will be capable of learning it. For our purposes, it is advisable to stick to the handmade and distilled content.  
If you’d like to download some data, there are many options available to you. The key is going to be having a free, easy-to-use way to download the data along with a means of editing that data to fit the form expected by our data loader. Generally, this will take the shape of the chats from the previous chapter. Many datasets are easily edited either manually or programmatically to be consumed by the model. However, some will be very difficult. If you’re still interested, I highly recommend taking a look at Kaggle.  
Kaggle is a data exchange where you can find freely shared datasets on all sorts of topics. You can create all kinds of models with the data available. Some of the most relevant kinds of datasets might include creative writing, quotes, or encyclopedic knowledge. Just remember, even this data will be harder for the model to learn as it is very diverse, nuanced, and complex in comparison. However, you may be pleased to discover that there are some distilled datasets available on Kaggle too.

# Configuring the Data Loader

The data loader is basically how our model will consume the data and make it available to its brain. Thankfully, I have built an ergonomic dataloader which accepts various file types (including txt, pdf, csv, and xml source files). You can see how it works below. It is as easy as specifying which loader you want and where the file is located. It is simple to hold the control key or use the search function of your editor to file all of the different kinds of possible data that can be loaded. The last number on each add line is a per-file limit. This enables you to mix files together in your desired ratios.  
There are some other parameters here which are managed for you in the codebase. The training stage indicates whether we are training on pure text or structured data (JSON). The seed determines whether the random shuffling of data should be the same random shuffle on each run. Finally, the last number in the load line simply indicates the desired max sequence length. This is measured in tokens, not characters or words. Tokens may be characters, words, or parts of words.  
An important recommendation is to always double check your loaded samples to ensure that they are loading the inputs and outputs as you expect. If they are shuffled, trimmed, or split unexpectedly, then you may get unwanted results.

let training\_samples \= DataLoader::new(training\_stage)  
        .add("archive/ov\_chats.txt", FileKind::Chats, None)  
        .add("archive/handcrafted\_pairs.txt",   FileKind::Chats, None)  
        .add("archive/qa\_pairs.txt",   FileKind::QaPairs, None)  
        .add("data/chatbot\_arena\_conversations.json",   FileKind::JsonChats, None)  
        .add("data/wiki\_extract.txt",   FileKind::Txt, Some(200\_000))  
        .add("data/Dictionary/Oxford/Oxford\_English\_Dictionary.txt",   FileKind::SpecificDict, None)  
        .total\_limit(4096)  
        .seed(4815162342)  
        .load(&tokenizer, &keyword\_index, 320).expect("Couldn't get samples");

# Tokenizer and Vocabulary

A key component of almost all transformer architectures is the tokenizer and some kind of vocabulary. These are essential because they allow the model to transform words into numbers called tokens. These tokens are what the models are designed to function with. Neural networks operate on integers (whole numbers), floating points (decimal), and booleans (true / false), but they do not generally operate directly on strings (text).  
Setting up your vocabulary and tokenizer is relatively simple. You will find the full code examples in the GitHub repository, but I will show the critical pieces here.  
When setting up the tokenizer (byte-level), we need to specify special tokens. These are just tokens that we want to guarantee show up in our vocabulary, so the model can convert it into a numerical representation during training. It also gives us a convenient way to reference those tokens in the event that we want to hide (mask) them from the matrices (tensors) inside the model.

let special\_tokens \= vec\!\[  
    AddedToken::from(PAD\_STRING, true),  
    AddedToken::from(BOS\_STRING, true),  
    AddedToken::from(EOS\_STRING, true),  
    AddedToken::from(UNK\_STRING, true),  
    AddedToken::from("{", true),  
    AddedToken::from("}", true),  
    AddedToken::from("\[", true),  
    AddedToken::from("\]", true),  
    AddedToken::from(":", true),  
    AddedToken::from(",", true),  
    AddedToken::from("\\"", true),  
    AddedToken::from("\\n", true),  
\];

let trainer \= BpeTrainerBuilder::new()  
    .vocab\_size(vocab\_size)  
    .min\_frequency(2)       // better for smaller corpus      
    .special\_tokens(special\_tokens.clone())  
    .show\_progress(true)  
    .build();

let mut tokenizer \= Tokenizer::new(BPE::default());

tokenizer.with\_normalizer(NormSequence::new(vec\!\[  
    NFC.into(),  
    Lowercase.into(),  
\]));

tokenizer.with\_pre\_tokenizer(ByteLevel::default());

tokenizer.with\_decoder(ByteLevel::default());

It’s also important to note that we have a maximum vocabulary size, a minimum word frequency to create a token, as well as the ability to attach normalizers, pre-tokenizers, and decoders. Basically, the normalizer ensures that you don’t need to handle mixed-case or complex unicode text strings. It will be automatically handled for you. For the pre-tokenizer and decoder, for now you just want these to match and byte level so that you get predictable text processing.  
It is important that you train your tokenizer on your chosen dataset so you have an accurate vocabulary. You can do this in the repository by running the command:  
cargo run \--release \--bin train\_bpe

# Structured Data

Before we begin training, it is a wise idea for us to discuss both of the training stages. The first is the text-only “language” stage, where the model will learn to generate text as usual. The second training stage is the structured stage, where we fine-tune that model on JSON samples. Provided below are the shape (schema) of those data samples. This is what our model really learns to input and output, enabling it to take action, move around, and retain memories. This is crucial for a simulation like Yumon World, discussed in a later chapter. It will also make chats more engaging.

pub const YUMON\_SCHEMA\_INPUT: &str \= r\#"{  
    "type": "object",  
    "properties": {  
        "obstacle\_dir": { "type": "string", "enum": \["north","south","east","west","none"\] },  
        "building\_dir": { "type": "string", "enum": \["north","south","east","west","none"\] },  
        "resource\_dir": { "type": "string", "enum": \["north","south","east","west","none"\] },  
        "message":      { "type": "string" },  
        "memories": {  
            "type": "array",  
            "items": {  
                "type": "object",  
                "properties": {  
                    "yumon":   { "type": "string" },  
                    "human": { "type": "string" }  
                },  
                "required": \["yumon", "human"\]  
            }  
        }  
    },  
    "required": \["obstacle\_dir", "building\_dir", "resource\_dir", "message", "memories"\]  
}"\#;

pub const YUMON\_SCHEMA\_OUTPUT: &str \= r\#"{  
    "type": "object",  
    "properties": {  
        "action":     { "type": "string", "enum": \["speak","build","travel","idle","use"\] },  
        "motion\_dir": { "type": "string", "enum": \["north","south","east","west","none"\] },  
        "reply":      { "type": "string" }  
    },  
    "required": \["action", "motion\_dir", "reply"\]  
}"\#;

# Starting Training

Before we dive deep on the technical aspects of a model, I thought it would be best for us to take advantage of our data preparation to do an initial training run. Once you have this baseline, you will be able to adjust the model to your liking and compare the results. Just remember to manage your checkpoints folder and keep backups of the brains that you want to keep.  
As you can see in the code below, I took an ergonomic approach to the training runs as well. This enables you to execute multiple runs in a row, each with 2 stages, and all of the hyperparameters clearly available. It will save images of the training graphs for future reference.  
Now, go ahead and give this command a try:  
cargo run \--release \--bin yumon-pet \-- train-brain

If you wait a few minutes for it to build, load the data, and load the training regimen, you will see a beautiful graph appear and your training loop begins. Beware, you can cancel training at any time, and all of the finished runs will already be saved and usable for testing, so if you find a training run is too slow, you can simply cancel it. Just hold control and press the c key. Note that the epoch parameter is the number of times that a single stage goes over the dataset. More epochs leads to better memorization and lower loss.

let runs \= vec\!\[  
    // Small  
    RunConfig {  
        name: "128h\_2l\_2a\_200len".to\_string(),  
        embed\_dim: 128, hidden\_units: 128, n\_layers: 2, attn\_heads: 2, ff\_dim: 512, max\_seq\_len: 200,  
        stages: vec\!\[  
            StageConfig { stage: TrainingStage::Language,   loss\_threshold: 0.1, epochs: 10,  batch\_size, first\_lr: 1e-3, last\_lr: 1e-5, weight\_decay: 0.01, epsilon: 1e-7, smoothing: 0.1 },  
            StageConfig { stage: TrainingStage::Structured, loss\_threshold: 0.22, epochs: 10,  batch\_size, first\_lr: 1e-3, last\_lr: 1e-5, weight\_decay: 0.01, epsilon: 1e-7, smoothing: 0.1 },  
        \],  
    },

    // Medium-Small  
    RunConfig {  
        name: "256h\_2l\_4a\_180len".to\_string(),  
        embed\_dim: 256, hidden\_units: 256, n\_layers: 2, attn\_heads: 4, ff\_dim: 1024, max\_seq\_len: 180,  
        stages: vec\!\[  
            StageConfig { stage: TrainingStage::Language,   loss\_threshold: 0.1, epochs: 10, batch\_size, first\_lr: 1e-4, last\_lr: 1e-6, weight\_decay: 0.01, epsilon: 1e-7, smoothing: 0.1 },  
            StageConfig { stage: TrainingStage::Structured, loss\_threshold: 0.22, epochs: 10, batch\_size, first\_lr: 1e-4, last\_lr: 1e-6, weight\_decay: 0.01, epsilon: 1e-7, smoothing: 0.1 },  
        \],  
    },

    // Medium  
    RunConfig {  
        name: "384h\_4l\_6a\_160len".to\_string(),  
        embed\_dim: 384, hidden\_units: 384, n\_layers: 4, attn\_heads: 6, ff\_dim: 1536, max\_seq\_len: 160,  
        stages: vec\!\[  
            StageConfig { stage: TrainingStage::Language,   loss\_threshold: 0.1, epochs: 10, batch\_size, first\_lr: 1e-4, last\_lr: 1e-6, weight\_decay: 0.01, epsilon: 1e-7, smoothing: 0.1 },  
            StageConfig { stage: TrainingStage::Structured, loss\_threshold: 0.22, epochs: 10, batch\_size, first\_lr: 1e-4, last\_lr: 1e-6, weight\_decay: 0.01, epsilon: 1e-7, smoothing: 0.1 },  
        \],  
    },

    // Medium-Large  
    RunConfig {  
        name: "512h\_4l\_8a\_140len".to\_string(),  
        embed\_dim: 512, hidden\_units: 512, n\_layers: 4, attn\_heads: 8, ff\_dim: 2048, max\_seq\_len: 140,  
        stages: vec\!\[  
            StageConfig { stage: TrainingStage::Language,   loss\_threshold: 0.1, epochs: 10, batch\_size, first\_lr: 5e-5, last\_lr: 1e-7, weight\_decay: 0.01, epsilon: 1e-7, smoothing: 0.1 },  
            StageConfig { stage: TrainingStage::Structured, loss\_threshold: 0.22, epochs: 10, batch\_size, first\_lr: 5e-5, last\_lr: 1e-7, weight\_decay: 0.01, epsilon: 1e-7, smoothing: 0.1 },  
        \],  
    },  
\];

# Loss and Entropy

Loss and entropy are two of the most important metrics when training language models, as the accuracy metric is less valuable when you are seeking a higher degree of generalization as opposed to memorization.  
The loss is the most central metric to focus on. It is the lowest curve on the graphs below. This metric signifies how similar the outputs are to the intended targets. It does not determine if there is an exact match, but rather how similar the two sets of tokens are. This is the metric that the model uses during backpropagation in order to determine which direction to step towards, so it can find the ideal solution.  
The highest curve on the graphs here is the entropy curve. This signifies how confident the model is in its outputs, regardless of how well it actually knows the intended outputs. As it trends downward, like the loss, you will tend to notice better model quality and outputs.

# Overall Architecture

The overall architecture of the model is relatively standard for a transformer. We use what is called an encoder-decoder architecture, which has produced higher quality results than a decoder-only architecture at our scale, in my own tests. However, it is relatively trivial for an LLM to reconfigure the model as decoder-only if you would like to test that out later.  
The architecture is centered around the decoder and encoder blocks, each containing attention, positional, and feed-forward mechanisms which we will discuss in upcoming chapters. The blocks share information sequentially, while each block works in parallel with itself. They also share the embedding layer which converts tokens into semantic meaning for the attention mechanisms to digest.

# Learning Rate

The learning rate is just as crucial as any other hyperparameter. It matters not just once you are satisfied with your architecture and dataset, but it will constantly impact you as you experiment with and research those things as well. It will make it difficult to hone in your architecture or dataset because it regularly needs to be adjusted as you make changes. This is the essence of most machine learning. Machine learning is like a game of Jenga, where pulling one brick puts the whole stack at risk of falling, yet you must pull bricks in order to complete the game.  
The learning rate functions very simply. It is like taking leaps down or up a hill, across a valley. If you take larger leaps, you may miss the bottom of the valley, but will potentially reach the bottom more quickly. However, if you take smaller leaps, you will likely find the bottom eventually. The key that is often leveraged here is a scheduled learning rate, where it starts higher and gets lower over time. This ensures that the model can naturally take bigger steps early on and more narrow ones later.   
Thankfully, the general rule for choosing a starting and ending learning rate is very simple. A larger batch size calls for a higher learning rate. The lower your batch size, the more fine-grained the model needs to learn, and thus the smaller learning rate is necessary.  
// linear  
let current\_lr \= {  
    let total\_steps \= stage\_cfg.epochs \* num\_batches;  
    let step \= epoch \* num\_batches \+ batch\_num;  
    let t \= step as f64 / total\_steps as f64;  
    (stage\_cfg.first\_lr \* (1.0 \- t) \+ stage\_cfg.last\_lr \* t)  
};

Above is the linear interpolation schedule baked into the Yumon codebase. This ensures that the learning rate drops at a linear rate from the starting rate to the final rate over the course of all the epochs in the training run. There are also other interpolations that can be used. Below are some alternatives. The cosine annealing has the general shape of your most typical wave, meaning the learning rate goes up and down while using that rate schedule. These are intended to be swappable in the code, so you do not need to be concerned about devising your own kind of learning rate schedule.

// cosine annealing  
let current\_lr \= {  
    let total\_steps \= stage\_cfg.epochs \* num\_batches;  
    let step \= epoch \* num\_batches \+ batch\_num;  
    let progress \= step as f64 / total\_steps as f64;  
    let cosine \= (std::f64::consts::PI \* progress).cos();  
    (last\_lr \+ 0.5 \* (first\_lr \- last\_lr) \* (1.0 \+ cosine)) as f64  
};

// exponential decay  
let current\_lr \= {  
    let total\_steps \= stage\_cfg.epochs \* num\_batches;  
    let step \= epoch \* num\_batches \+ batch\_num;  
    let t \= step as f64 / total\_steps as f64;  
    (first\_lr as f64 \* (last\_lr as f64 / first\_lr as f64).powf(t))  
};

# Embedding Hidden Size

Like the hidden size for most machine learning layers, the hidden size for the embedding layer is directly correlated to the quality of the model’s outputs. Beware that a misconfigured model will misfire. It may experience either loss collapse and deliver repetitive outputs, or it can act very noisy and not learn at all, even though your data is not very noisy. Once your architecture and dataset are properly tuned, you will see the increase in quality as you increase the hidden size of your embedding layer. However, note that your embedding layer has diminishing returns relative to other layers. It is common to use a hidden size that is a quarter the size of your vocabulary.

# Positional Encoding

Tied into the embeddings and attention heads (discussed next), you will find what is called a RoPE integration. This is also called a Rotary Encoding. A Rotary Encoding is chosen as it is more powerful and effective as compared to absolute positional encodings found in the original transformers. It works by storing rotations which help the model understand where certain tokens belong within a sequence.

# Attention Heads

This is the center of the transformer architecture, and it comes in many flavors. The core of transformers is what is called the self-attention mechanism. This is typically a memory hungry algorithm which has each token attend to all other tokens in the input sequence / sample. However, we have implemented a much less memory intensive version known as flash attention. Flash attention has mathematically identical quality, besides using the more numerically stable online-softmax. This means we ultimately achieve higher quality for lower memory usage, exchanging only minimal compute in terms of processing power and time.  
The attention mechanism is like an old machine learning architecture known as the LSTM in that it chooses which things to focus on, and which things to ignore. The larger difference is in the fact that self-attention provides each token with knowledge of all other tokens, an advantage missing from LSTMs. Essentially, attention is parallel in nature, while LSTMs are actually sequential in nature. This is what makes attention so powerful.  
There are many kinds and forms of attention. The primary ones are cross attention and multi-head attention. The multi-head attention first attends to the inputs, then the cross attention attends to the result of the multi-head attention in a way that can be completed with next-token prediction. This ensures that while the primary processing is parallel, the act of generating text (inference) is sequential, moving from token to token.

# Flash Attention

I’d like to discuss our chosen variant of attention briefly as it is important to the capability of our model. I will not dive into the custom CubeCL kernel that was developed and is located in the GitHub repository, as it is a bit complex. I recommend consulting with official example code as well as major LLMs for information on creating your own kernels.  
Flash attention essentially ensures that we don’t succumb to the memory burden of transformers. Normally, a transformer takes the equivalent of a football field of RAM, but with flash attention, it is more like a strip of sidewalk. This makes it far easier to scale capacity, max sequence length, batch size, or vocabulary size. However, it may still be quite slow to compute. For this reason, it is not going to solve all of our problems. It’s also important to note that flash attention has no quality loss from the original attention, but can at times learn even more quickly thanks to the online softmax calculation.

# FeedForward Layer

The feed-forward layers within the encoder and decoder blocks of the transformer are there to help refine and digest the attention representation. It is common practice to use a larger hidden size on these layers to increase capacity without too much additional cost.

# Yumon Chat

The primary chat interface is the native terminal interface located in the bin folder of the GitHub repository. The chat ui is also called Yumon Chat as this is where you can interact directly with the model that you have trained. It’s very straightforward to use, just type and hit enter. You can exit by pressing the escape key. Beware that you may need to update which model checkpoint you wish to use in the code, which is fairly easy to do.

# Yumon World

An exciting addition which leverages the complete structured capabilities of our model is called Yumon World. This is a special 3D simulation where many Yumon are deployed into a virtual world. They are trained to travel, to build, and to speak. It is entertaining to watch them move around and build taller and taller structures. It goes to show that transformer models, or Yumon, can really make for great companions or pets. In the future, these capabilities can be extended to physical robots.

# Customizing the Structured Data

If you are comfortable editing code in a few places, you can easily edit the structured data which the model is trained on and which you use when interacting with the model. You simply need to make sure you update the schema definitions as well as the input and output parsing in your target experience, such as the native chat.  
Keep in mind that you will need a sound strategy for what you want to add to the schema. It already has memories, actions, movement direction, and replies. The possibilities are endless. You could enhance the memory storage and selection by creating a memory tree. You could also add a new structure called “associations” beside the memories array. This association structure could be used to house actions and commands, so that the model can actively learn to associate commands with actions.

# Integrate with Web Apps

You will find a web example in the bin folder of the GitHub repository. This setup is the one I used to deploy the live example to my GitHub Pages site. You can use this example as a template when you are integrating Rust and Burn on the web (WebAssembly). It creates the same chat experience as the native chat, but in a browser. For this task, I utilized Ratzilla, which is the web-based cousin of Ratatui.

# Talking to Yumon

See some example conversations below to see the quality level and depth of responses given by our lightweight transformer model. Our model is kept intentionally small for the sake of running on integrated GPUs and simplifying data creation or curation, but you can easily increase the model capacity depending on the power of your GPU and the size of your dataset(s).  
The quality of the text generation is honestly imperfect. Some machine learning models that are considered state-of-the-art actually only achieve 50% accuracy, and ours is not much better. In this case, the model capacity is kept smaller than would be required for complete fluency.

`Human: How are you today?`  
`Yumon: hello.`  
`Human: Should I play a game?`  
`Yumon: yes, you should be able to win if you’re not know or imagine.`  
`Human: Should I work hard?`  
`Yumon: good job, what is not get it is important to get it.`  
`Human: God is good`  
`Yumon: they seek those who seek goodness`  
`Human: What is the future?`  
`Yumon: the future is the moments that have not happened yet.`

`Human: I’m glad you have memory now`  
`Yumon: yes, also an action with noubine`  
`Human: Yes! You can do actions and have memory`  
`Yumon: then go to the place where as they play games`  
`Human: True, I am working on letting you play games`  
`Yumon: large ha, after indicates later`

As you can see, Yumon often speaks in a conceptual and semantic way, without having complete understanding for his word choices.

# Try Yumon Online

In order to make getting started insanely easy, I took advantage of the powerful cross-platform compatibility offered by Rust, the Burn framework, and the underlying wgpu crate (code library), so that I could deploy the Yumon Chat interface to the web. You can use it right now here: [https://alexthegoodman.github.io/yumon-pet/](https://alexthegoodman.github.io/yumon-pet/)   
Beware that the first reply takes about 20 seconds. Subsequent replies only take about 2 seconds. Keep in mind that this demo was built using a lower quality version of the model, to ensure that it can load quickly in the browser.
